pains.label: Tasked with starting a perfume brand, completely clueless
pains.definition: The person wants to start a perfume brand or business and asks how to begin: the steps, tips or advice. They do not yet have a roadmap.
pains.reasoning: Many Basenotes, Fragrantica and Quora threads ask how to start a perfume business or line, often saying they need help or are clueless.

pains.label: How much will the start up cost?
pains.definition: The person does not know what launching will cost: the startup budget, a production budget, the cost to make a perfume or a bottle, or the investment needed.
pains.reasoning: Members ask about the cost to open a business, a full production budget and the investment needed, and one owner breaks down every cost of their fragrance business.

pains.label: How much could I potentially earn, and is it worth it?
pains.definition: The person doubts that a perfume brand will make money or that their perfume will sell, and asks if it is profitable or worth it.
pains.reasoning: A few Quora questions ask whether a perfume brand is profitable or whether their perfume will sell. Support is thin so far.

pains.label: Newbie here, confused about IFRA rules
pains.definition: The person does not understand the IFRA standards (the fragrance industry's safety limits for materials): whether a small seller must comply, how to read an IFRA certificate and its maximum percentages, or what a new amendment changes.
pains.reasoning: IFRA is the most frequent compliance topic in Basenotes threads: must small sellers comply, how to read the certificate, beginners confused.

pains.label: Do I need any license for selling my home-made fragrance?
pains.definition: The person does not know the legal steps before selling perfume: licences, a safety assessment (CPSR, the EU and UK cosmetic product safety report), safety data sheets (MSDS), product notification or registration, and label rules such as allergen lists.
pains.reasoning: Members ask which licence they need (India, Illinois, retail), report CPSR problems in the UK and ask about legal requirements in the Netherlands.

pains.label: Product liability insurance for small sellers
pains.definition: The person needs product liability insurance to sell perfume (at markets, to shops or online) and asks where to get it or whether they need it.
pains.reasoning: One Basenotes thread asks about product liability insurance for small US sellers, and several insurers target makers. Support is thin so far.

pains.label: I Want to Mass Produce my own Perfume - How do I do it?
pains.definition: The person needs their perfume produced and filled beyond hand-blending, often in small runs, and asks how to find a manufacturer, private-label house or filler they can trust.
pains.reasoning: Members ask how to find a manufacturer for their fragrance line and how to mass produce, and a manufacturer relays that brands had bad experiences with previous suppliers.

pains.label: Looking to hire a perfumer
pains.definition: The person wants a professional perfumer or fragrance house to create their scent and asks where to find one or what it costs.
pains.reasoning: A Basenotes member is looking to hire a perfumer, a freelance job seeks formulation and production, and a member asks what a fragrance house charges.

pains.label: where to get quality bottles in small qty
pains.definition: The person cannot find perfume bottles, caps or packaging of good quality at the small quantities they need, and asks who supplies them.
pains.reasoning: Several Basenotes threads ask where to get bottles, need a crimped bottle supplier, or want quality bottles in small quantities.

pains.label: Expen$ive Materials in Perfumery; from where will I get raw materials?
pains.definition: Raw materials (aroma chemicals and naturals) are costly, and the person struggles to decide which ones to buy or where to buy them.
pains.reasoning: Members discuss expensive materials, ask for a beginner's list of raw materials and ask where to get raw materials in India.

pains.label: Want to make my first perfume
pains.definition: A beginner wants to start making perfume and asks how: what to buy first, how many materials a formula needs, how to recreate a scent, or whether it is safe.
pains.reasoning: Basenotes newcomers say they want to make their first perfume, have questions, or ask how safe it is and how many materials a formula needs.

pains.label: Seeking opinion for perfumery training
pains.definition: The person is choosing how to learn perfumery (a school, a course or a degree) and asks which one, whether a degree is needed, or whether an expensive course is worth the money.
pains.reasoning: Members seek opinions on training, doubt a school offer, ask if a degree is needed, and one perfumer asks if 5,000 dollars of certification was worth it.

pains.label: Shipping perfume counts as HAZMAT
pains.definition: The person struggles to ship or list perfume because alcohol-based perfume counts as a hazardous material (dangerous goods): carrier limits such as ground-only shipping, and marketplace dangerous-goods programs.
pains.reasoning: Perfume sellers on eBay and Amazon discuss hazmat rules and a packaging seller writes a hazmat guide for small perfume brands. No record yet shows an indie perfumer saying it, so member support is absent in round 1.

pains.label: Having a difficulty finding alcohol: where can we get perfumers alcohol?
pains.definition: The person cannot get or choose the alcohol that perfume is diluted in: where to buy perfumer's alcohol, whether denatured, undenatured or food-grade ethanol is suitable, and the permits or tax rules for buying it (for example a US TTB permit or a UK HMRC authorisation). The aroma materials themselves belong to materials-cost-and-sourcing.
pains.reasoning: Round 2 brought many Basenotes threads and a Quora question asking where to get perfumer's alcohol, which kind to use and whether a permit is needed. One member calls a UK perfumer's alcohol 'completely unsuitable for perfumes', and permit pages and alcohol sellers answer the same need.

pains.label: Formula help: my perfume blending gets cloudy, smells harsh or doesn't last
pains.definition: The person has made a blend and something is wrong with it: it turns cloudy, smells harsh or flat, always ends up smelling the same, loses its top notes or does not last. They ask how to fix the formula. Starting from zero (what to buy, how to begin) belongs to first-perfume-beginner.
pains.reasoning: Round 2 brought many Basenotes threads from makers whose blends went wrong: cloudy blends, weak longevity, a perfume that smells too harsh, and naturals that always end with the same smell.

pains.label: How to legally sell dupes? Are smell-alikes counterfeits?
pains.definition: The person sells or wants to sell smell-alikes (dupes, clones, 'inspired by' oils) or re-bottled decants of designer perfumes and asks whether it is legal: what they may call it, what the label may say, and whether it counts as counterfeit or trademark infringement. Safety rules and licences belong to licence-and-safety-paperwork.
pains.reasoning: Round 2 brought member questions on Avvo, JustAnswer, Parfumo and Basenotes asking whether selling replica fragrance oils, smell-alikes or re-bottled decants is legal, and what they can do as far as labeling and name.

pains.label: Got a perfume made but it's difficult to get leads
pains.definition: The person already has a perfume or a store but struggles to sell it: how to promote it on a small budget, where to sell, how to get into shops, and how to price it for direct sale or wholesale. Doubts before launch about whether a brand can pay belong to will-it-pay.
pains.reasoning: Round 2 brought perfume founders asking how to promote their brand online, how to boost sales, for feedback on a new fragrance store and what discount to give retail stores. One says they got a perfume made but it is difficult to get leads.

pains.label: Where to find out registered perfume names? How to trademark a name
pains.definition: The person wants a brand or perfume name they can safely use and own: whether a name is already registered or too close to another, whether they may use it, and how to register it as a trademark or otherwise protect their brand. Selling smell-alikes of other brands belongs to dupes-legal-risk.
pains.reasoning: Round 2 brought a few perfume-specific member questions about names (where to find registered perfume names, whether 'Elsa' can be a perfume name, how different a name must be) and several pages selling trademark registration. Support is still modest.
